# 11.1 Backtesting {background-color="#16181A" style="color:#F7F6F3"}

## Three valid designs

Random K-fold CV is invalid whenever observations are ordered in time.

::: {.tight}
- **Rolling origin, expanding window** — train on $1..t$, predict $t+h$, increment $t$. Uses all
  history; training size grows, so early and late errors are not comparable.
- **Rolling origin, fixed window** — train on $t-w..t$. Constant training size; adapts to structural
  change; discards old information.
- **Blocked CV with a purge and an embargo** — leave a gap of at least $h$ observations between train
  and test.
:::

## Why the purge matters

A gap prevents leakage through **overlapping horizons** or through **serially correlated features**.

::: {.check}
Essential whenever features are constructed from rolling windows — which, in macro work, is almost
always.
:::

## Two rules violated constantly

**1. Point-in-time data.** Macroeconomic series are **revised**. A backtest using today's vintage of
GDP gives your model information no forecaster had at the time.

::: {.check}
Use real-time vintages — ALFRED, or the Philadelphia Fed's real-time dataset — or **state clearly
that you have not**.
:::

## The second rule

**2. Every preprocessing step must be inside the loop.**

::: {.tight}
- standardisation
- **factor extraction** — Session 08
- feature selection
- hyperparameter choice
:::

::: {.warn}
Extracting factors from the full sample and then backtesting is look-ahead bias. It is the single
most common flaw in student factor-model projects.
:::

# 11.2 Comparing honestly {background-color="#16181A" style="color:#F7F6F3"}

## Against a benchmark that is hard to beat

A random walk, an AR($p$), or the consensus forecast.

::: {.warn}
**A lower RMSE without a significance statement is an anecdote.**
:::

## Diebold–Mariano

Let $e_{1t}, e_{2t}$ be the forecast errors of two models and
$d_t = L(e_{1t}) - L(e_{2t})$ the loss differential. Under the null of equal predictive accuracy,
$\mathbb{E}[d_t] = 0$, and

$$\mathrm{DM} = \frac{\bar d}{\sqrt{\widehat{\operatorname{Var}}(\bar d)}} \;\xrightarrow{d}\; N(0,1)$$

## The variance must be HAC

Estimate $\widehat{\operatorname{Var}}(\bar d)$ with a **Newey–West** estimator, because $d_t$ is
serially correlated at multi-step horizons.

::: {.check}
Use a lag truncation of at least $h-1$.
:::

## Two cautions

::: {.tight}
- The test is **not valid for nested models** estimated on the same sample — use **Clark–West**.
- With small samples, the **Harvey–Leybourne–Newbold** correction is advisable.
:::

# 11.3 Distribution shift {background-color="#16181A" style="color:#F7F6F3"}

## Four kinds

| Type | What changes | Fix |
|---|---|---|
| **Covariate shift** | $P(X)$; $P(Y\mid X)$ stable | Importance weighting, or just retrain |
| **Label shift** | $P(Y)$; $P(X\mid Y)$ stable | Reweight, or correct the intercept (Session 06) |
| **Concept drift** | $P(Y\mid X)$ | Retraining necessary but not sufficient — the form may be wrong |
| **Feedback** | your model changes the world it predicts | Redesign |

## How to detect them

| Type | Detection |
|---|---|
| Covariate shift | Train a classifier to distinguish train from deploy |
| Label shift | Compare predicted marginal to observed |
| Concept drift | **Only** detectable once outcomes arrive |
| Feedback | Requires causal reasoning, not monitoring |

## The classifier diagnostic

Pool training and deployment features, label them by period, and try to predict the label.

> **If a classifier can tell your two periods apart, so can your model's errors.**

::: {.check}
AUC near 0.5 is reassuring. Near 1.0 is an alarm.
:::

## Goodhart's law, stated precisely

> When a measure becomes a target, the relationship the model learned between measure and outcome is
> exactly the relationship agents have an incentive to break.

::: {.muted}
A credit-scoring feature that predicts default only until applicants learn it is used is not a
stable feature.
:::

::: {.warn}
This is a **causal** problem (Session 10), not a monitoring problem. **No amount of retraining
solves it.**
:::

# 11.4 Model governance {background-color="#16181A" style="color:#F7F6F3"}

## Seven headings

A deployable model is accompanied by a document a competent successor could act on.

::: {.tight}
1. **Intended use** — and out-of-scope uses
2. **Data lineage** — sources, vintages, dates, licences, quality issues, checksums
3. **Preprocessing** — every transformation, in order, with the code
4. **Validation** — design, why the CV scheme matches deployment, metrics, benchmark, subgroups
5. **Limitations** — where it performs worst, who is under-represented, what is load-bearing
6. **Monitoring plan** — what is tracked, how often, what threshold triggers review
7. **Ownership** — who is accountable, and the **retirement criterion**
:::

## Not bureaucracy

::: {.check}
Sections **5** and **6** are where the intellectual content of the whole course finally has to be
written down for someone else.
:::

::: {.muted}
Template: [`02-lab/governance-file-template.md`](02-lab/governance-file-template.md)
:::

## Write a specific retirement trigger

::: {.warn}
A model with no stated retirement condition is never retired. It is used until something goes
visibly wrong — and by then it has been wrong for a while.
:::

> *"Retrain when the era-classifier AUC against the training period exceeds 0.75, or when rolling
> 2-year RMSE exceeds 1.4× the backtest median. Retire if retraining does not restore it."*

::: {.check}
Specific enough that someone who has never met you can execute it.
:::

# 11.5 The arc {background-color="#16181A" style="color:#F7F6F3"}

## The dial, and the self-deception it prevents

| Session | The dial | The self-deception |
|---|---|---|
| 2–3 | Which variables enter, how errors are modelled | "My standard errors are correct because the software printed them" |
| 4 | Model complexity, via CV | "It fits the data well" |
| 5–6 | $\lambda$ and $\alpha$ | "The model identified the true drivers" |
| 6 | The decision threshold | "It is 97% accurate" |

## Continued

| Session | The dial | The self-deception |
|---|---|---|
| 7 | Depth, learning rate, $m$ | "The important feature is the cause" |
| 8 | The number of factors | "I extracted factors, then backtested" |
| 9 | $k$, and the representation of text | "The algorithm found clusters, so clusters exist" |
| **10** | **Nothing — identification is not a dial** | "A better predictor is a better policy guide" |
| 11 | The monitoring threshold | "It worked last year" |

## The exception that defines the course

> **No tuning parameter buys you identification.**

::: {.check}
Session 10 is the one week with nothing to tune. That is not an omission — it is the point.
:::

# 11.6 Returning to *Europe 2031* {background-color="#16181A" style="color:#F7F6F3"}

## Sharper questions than in week one

The scenario's numbers were introduced in Session 01 as **parameters of a narrative**. You can now
interrogate them.

::: {.tight}
- What would a **factor model** (S08) say about how many independent dimensions "technological
  capacity" actually has? Is compute one factor, or a proxy for several?
- Is the labour-displacement mechanism a **prediction** or a **causal** claim (S10)? Which would you
  need to justify the narrative's policy responses?
:::

## And two more

::: {.tight}
- Its policy menu implies **decisions under cost asymmetry**. What are $c_{FP}$ and $c_{FN}$ for
  acting on a false signal of European decline versus missing a true one (S06)?
- Its indicators would be **monitored over years**. Which are vulnerable to **Goodhart**, and which
  to **concept drift** (S11)?
:::

## Why a stress test

> The purpose of a stress test is not to be right. It is to make you specify **what you would need
> to know.**

::: {.check}
That is also the purpose of a model — and it is what you will be examined on next week.
:::

# The lab {background-color="#16181A" style="color:#F7F6F3"}

## What you do

::: {.tight}
1. Backtest **your project's** model with a rolling origin, at the deployment horizon
2. Plot error by period and find the break
3. Run the era classifier; report the AUC and read it
4. Complete the governance file, including a **numeric** retirement trigger
:::

::: {.warn}
Every preprocessing step inside the loop — including factor extraction.
:::

## The two-minute report

::: {.tight}
1. **What I did** — the backtest design, the window, the horizon
2. **The number** — error against a hard benchmark, with a DM statement
3. **The catch** — what would make you retire this model
:::

::: {.check}
Session 12 is your defence. The governance file is what you will be asked about.
:::
